subject: [RFC PATCH] x86,resctrl: Read event counters with an IPI when the read cannot block

reviews.author: Reinette Chatre
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Reinette Chatre pointed out that the patch does not handle the case where CONFIG_RESCTRL_MON_READ_IRQSAFE is disabled, which would cause a regression on architectures other than x86.

Reviewer noted that the patch's solution for high-performance monitoring is overly aggressive, given the existing limitations of the resctrl mon_data files interface.

Reviewer Reinette Chatre asked Shakeel Butt to consider the thread that followed his previous proposal, implying that there may be relevant information or context that was not addressed in the current patch.

Reviewer Reinette Chatre noted that the proposed patch only slightly adjusts the limit of how many monitor groups this deployment can support, and suggested considering a per-group rate as proposed by Peter Newman to enable full capability of the systems.

Reviewer noted that reading 128 MON groups with interrupts off can take up to 131 us, which may be significant for applications where the kernel is also monitoring itself.

Reviewer questioned the necessity of reading event counters every 100 ms, suggesting that the overflow handler's one-second interval is sufficient for querying data

Reviewer noted that the patch does not fully address the scalability issue for large numbers of monitoring groups, and suggested considering per-group rate files as a potential solution.

Reviewer Reinette Chatre suggested avoiding a config option and instead making read_irq_safe a per-resource property, citing concerns about the scope of change as multiple architectural drivers are involved.

Reviewer noted that the patch's use of raw_ functions to disable preemption is only effective when preemption is disabled, and suggested it may be a re-implementation of smp_call_function_any()

Reviewer Reinette Chatre noted that the '!tick_nohz_full_cpu(this_cpu)' check in the patch defeats its own goal of preventing an IPI when a reader is pinned to the domain, and suggested reordering the logic to prefer the current CPU whenever it's in the domain, nohz_full or not.
sentiment_signals: scope of change will be significant
reviews.raw_body:
Hi Shakeel,

On 10/20/26 8:13 AM, Shakeel Butt wrote:

---

This is very demanding usage of an interface that cannot and has never 
intended to be fast.

---

Did you consider the thread that followed that proposal to learn why it did
not land?

---

The numbers make the contention clear. If I got the math right the "after"
is still about 10us per file and with 4us spent holding rdtgroup_mutex there
is still about 6us per file spent outside resctrl. I expect this is
taken up by the syscalls, the various kernfs allocations to manage the read
cycle, also a seq_buf allocation of a page (just to return a few bytes of data).

I do not think the 750 file example accurately captures how "bad" things
can get. From what I can tell this proposal only *slightly* adjusts the limit
of how many monitor groups this deployment can support.

My guess is that the 750 file example looks like possibly about 25 monitor
groups with three events each monitored across 10 domains.

The "after" value indicates that this deployment can now support more monitoring
groups. For example, 250 monitor groups with a pass over the increased number
of files taking about 74ms.

AMD can support 4096 monitor groups though so while this change is undeniably
an improvement, it does not address the foundational limitations of this
interface and does not enable this deployment to use full capability of
the systems.

If the goal is indeed to obtain accurate monitoring data at regular
intervals when using the stated hardware at its full capacity then
I would suggest that you consider the per-group rate files that Peter
settled on per
https://lore.kernel.org/all/CALPaoCgpnVORZfbKVLXDFUZvv8jhpShHPzB3cwdLTZQH1o9ULw@mail.gmail.com/

I actually cannot remember seeing an update on that work after he posted that
message and my assumption has been that that is what they have been using since
then.

Essentially the solution builds on the monitoring data already collected by the
per-domain overflow handler, it turns that data into a rate that user space can
read on demand without any IPI.

---

128 MON groups sound low - it looks like AMD has 4096 possible MON groups.

Interrupting a monitored application with interrupts off for so long
is significant for a fleet whose product is the monitored application.

---

Is it really needed to get the data every 100ms? The overflow handler runs
every second and the data could just be queried from it.

---

...

As I understand this patch slightly moves the needle on how many monitoring
groups this deployment can support. I do not believe this patch enables this
deployment to support all monitoring groups possible. 

Please do consider per-group rate files as discussed in the thread around [4].

Even so, surely this patch improves performance under some scenarios. We could continue
to consider it if you still believe it useful.

---

Please avoid a config option. This could be a per-resource property,
for example, rdt_resource::mon::read_irq_safe (I'll defer naming debates).
I'd recommend against an architectural helper like [4] since now that there
are multiple architectural drivers the scope of change will be significant since
it spans across branches that take different routes upstream.

---

hmmm ... this is meaningless without preemption disabled, no? Looks like this
uses raw_ to get around the CONFIG_DEBUG_PREEMPT check :(

On the face of this it seems to attempt a re-implementation of smp_call_function_any()?

---

Doesn't this "!tick_nohz_full_cpu(this_cpu)" check defeat one major goal of this
patch, which is to prevent an IPI if a reader pinned itself to the domain? A monitoring
data reader may very well pin itself to a CPU in the monitoring domain and be running
on a nohz_full CPU.

It looks like the rule should be "prefer the current CPU whenever it is in the domain,
nohz_full or not"?

On first glance I wonder if this could be re-ordered. I surely need to think about this
more but how about something like below:


	if (r->mon.read_irq_safe) {
                  /*
                   * Reading the counter does not sleep, it only has to run on a
                   * CPU in the domain. Prefer the current CPU when it is one:
                   * the counter can be read without an IPI and without
                   * disturbing any other CPU. A nohz_full current CPU is not
                   * avoided, the reasons to avoid nohz_full CPUs, interrupting
                   * user space and queueing work that may never run, do not
                   * apply to the CPU making this request.
                   *
                   * Preemption is disabled for the test because the answer is
                   * only valid while this task cannot migrate. It is enabled
                   * again before the IPI to let other work run while waiting.
                   */
                  cpu = get_cpu();
                  if (!cpumask_test_cpu(cpu, cpumask))
                          cpu = cpumask_any_housekeeping(cpumask,
                                                         RESCTRL_PICK_ANY_CPU);
                  put_cpu();

                  smp_call_function_single(cpu, mon_event_count, rr, 1);
                  goto out_ctx_free;
          }

          cpu = cpumask_any_housekeeping(cpumask, RESCTRL_PICK_ANY_CPU);		
	 ...

2026-10-21.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new configuration option CONFIG_RESCTRL_MON_READ_IRQSAFE to allow reading event counters with interrupts off on the current CPU or using an IPI when necessary. This is done to reduce long stalls caused by readers sleeping while holding rdtgroup_mutex, which can lead to gaps in monitoring data. The patch adds support for x86 architecture and provides results showing a significant reduction in hold time per read and time off CPU while holding the mutex.

reviews.author: Peter Newman
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Peter Newman noted that the patch does not handle the case where the target CPU is in a nohz_full domain, and requested that an IPI be sent to wake up the kworker on the target CPU.

Reviewer Peter Newman expressed concerns about the practicality of implementing the patch, citing existing issues with MBM implementations on AMD and a preference to use the offcore PMU instead.

Reviewer pointed out that interrupt masking has a limited impact on latency since interrupts are reenabled between counter reads, and instead highlighted the issue of workload scheduling being impacted by this feature, suggesting it would need to be disabled in nohz_full mode for high-availability products.
reviews.raw_body:
On Thu, Oct 22, 2026 at 12:58 AM Reinette Chatre
<reinette.chatre@intel.com> wrote:

---

These changes have been available within Google for a while, but I
don't believe they've ever gone into use. They've had a lot of other
issues with the MBM implementations on AMD and have been estimating
jobs' bandwidth using the offcore PMU instead.

Shakeel, I can share the changes for you to try out, but they won't be
up to the standard for code review. If it works for you, that would be
one confirmed user and I could put more time into it.

---

Interrupts are reenabled between counter reads, so the cumulative time
interrupts are masked doesn't impact latency.

The time the customer's workload wasn't scheduled was a bigger issue,
though. On the higher-availability products, this was feature would
need to be disabled by an entire domain running in nohz_full mode.

-Peter

2026-10-22.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new configuration option CONFIG_RESCTRL_MON_READ_IRQSAFE to allow reading event counters with interrupts off on the current CPU or using an IPI when necessary. This is done to reduce long stalls caused by readers sleeping while holding rdtgroup_mutex, which can lead to gaps in monitoring data. The patch adds support for x86 architecture and provides results showing a significant reduction in hold time per read and time off CPU while holding the mutex.

reviews.author: Shakeel Butt (author)
reviews.summary:
Author acknowledged that the current implementation of CONFIG_RESCTRL_MON_READ_IRQSAFE does not handle the case where every CPU in the domain is nohz_full and agreed to add a check for this condition.

Author acknowledged that a critical reader of the interface is experiencing multi-second stalls, which causes gaps in system observability, and agreed to address this issue.

Author acknowledges the reviewer's concern about potential performance impact, but prioritizes avoiding critical daemons being stuck behind lower-priority readers.

The author acknowledges that the patch does not address scalability issues, but explains that its purpose is to reduce hold time and uncertainty by changing how locks are held during sleeping.

Author acknowledged the need to address the rate file interface and agreed to review Peter's prototype.

Author acknowledges that some userspace applications may be impacted by the proposed change, but notes that other applications like below and dynolog read less often and are not as affected.

Author acknowledges that the existing rate file tools are complementary to the mon_data files and agrees to address all reviewer suggestions in the next patch version.
reviews.raw_body:
Hi Reinette,

Thanks for the detailed review and feedback and sorry for late response.

On Wed, Oct 21, 2026 at 03:58:38PM -0700, Reinette Chatre wrote:

---

I think I agree here and I should have been more clear about my motivation. The
actual issue I am trying to resolve is that one of the reader of this interface
(actually below) is very critical for reliability of the system (or actually
observability) and we are seeing multi-second stalls in that daemon on this
interface. This causes gaps in our observability into the issues.

Also I think the read rates are modest. Below reads the whole tree every 5
seconds and scx_layered reads one root-group file per domain every 100ms.

[...]

---

Yes and I think the problem I am tring to solve is a bit different. I am ok with
spending more cpu cycles in order to avoid critical daemon getting stuck behind
lower priority readers and may get impacted by scheduling delays or priority
inversion.

---

Yes you are right. The patch does not change how a full sweep scales. It is only
changing the potential hold time of the sleeping locks and today it depends on
scheduling on another CPU which introduced a lot of uncertainty.

---

I will think more about rate file interface. It seems like Peter has offered his
prototype, I will take a look.

---

Most probably not. I have to check with scx_layered folks if they really need 100ms.
However below and dynolog reads less often and are impacted by stalls on this
path most of the time.

---

I will and I still feel the rate file are complementary as the existing tools
use the mon_data files and this patch helps them.

I will address all of your suggestions/concerns on the code in the next version.

Again, thanks a lot of the detailed and helpful feedback.

2026-10-26.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new configuration option CONFIG_RESCTRL_MON_READ_IRQSAFE to allow reading event counters with interrupts off on the current CPU or using an IPI when necessary. This is done to reduce long stalls caused by readers sleeping while holding rdtgroup_mutex, which can lead to gaps in monitoring data. The patch adds support for x86 architecture and provides results showing a significant reduction in hold time per read and time off CPU while holding the mutex.
